missing_spec_content.spec_text: Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction. ... The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says that the force between a magnet and an induced magnet or magnetic material is always attraction. Only permanent magnets can repel. This is a standard exam point.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: explain how the behaviour of a magnetic compass is related to evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says only 'Earth acts like a giant bar magnet'. It never explains that a compass points north anywhere on Earth with no other magnet nearby, which is evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic. It also never says that 'A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson links strength to how close the field lines are and says it is strongest near the poles. It never states directly that the field gets weaker further from the magnet.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: describe how the magnetic effect of a current can be demonstrated
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson mentions Ørsted's discovery but gives no demonstration method. For example, it does not describe a plotting compass deflecting near a current-carrying wire, or iron filings or compasses around a wire through card.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Shaping a wire to form a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field created by a current through the wire. ... explain how a solenoid arrangement can increase the magnetic effect of the current.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says the field inside a solenoid is 'uniform and strong'. It never states that coiling the wire increases the field strength, and never explains why: the fields from each turn add together and reinforce one another inside the coil.

above_gcse.text: Flux density — A measure of the strength of a magnetic field — stronger where field lines are closer
above_gcse.why: Magnetic flux density is not in these specification sections. It belongs to the Higher-tier motor effect content, and it is introduced here without units or context.

above_gcse.text: Thinking a DC current can work in a transformer. Transformers only work with AC. A steady DC makes a constant magnetic field. No change means no induced EMF.
above_gcse.why: Transformers and induced EMF are not in these sections and are not taught anywhere in this lesson. This could confuse the student.

above_gcse.text: MRI scanners: extremely powerful superconducting electromagnets are cooled to near absolute zero. They make fields strong enough to line up hydrogen atoms in the body.
above_gcse.why: Superconductivity and the alignment of nuclei in MRI go well beyond the specification. This is repeated in keyTerms 'Superconducting' and in writeBullets.

above_gcse.text: Loudspeakers: a permanent magnet and an electromagnet (the voice coil) push on each other. This moves a cone back and forth, making sound waves.
above_gcse.why: Loudspeakers are a motor-effect application (later Physics-only content). They are not part of the sections being taught.

above_gcse.text: Doubling the turns doubles the field, and halving the current halves it. These two changes cancel out.
above_gcse.why: The specification does not list number of turns as a factor and does not require proportional reasoning about solenoid field strength. The proportionality also only holds if the solenoid length is unchanged.

factual_errors.text: A permanent magnet is a material that is always magnetic. ... Examples include iron, cobalt, nickel and neodymium alloys.
factual_errors.correction: Iron, cobalt and nickel are magnetic materials, not permanent magnets in themselves. Iron especially is magnetically soft and does not keep its magnetism, which the lesson itself says. A permanent magnet 'produces its own magnetic field'. The same error appears in writeBullets[0] and in the tables[0] 'Materials' row.
Neodymium magnets are a neodymium–iron–boron alloy, not 'neodymium steel'. Pure iron is not a permanent magnet material.
An induced magnet is not necessarily weaker than the field that induces it. For example, a soft iron core greatly strengthens a solenoid's field, as keyPoints[2] says.

factual_errors.text: All other materials, like aluminium, copper, wood and plastic, are non-magnetic. Magnetic fields do not affect them.
factual_errors.correction: Non-magnetic materials are not attracted to magnets. However, magnetic fields can still affect them: a current-carrying copper wire feels a force in a field, which the lesson itself states in keyPoints[1]. Some materials are also very weakly magnetic.

factual_errors.text: Only iron, cobalt, nickel and steel are ferromagnetic.
factual_errors.correction: The specification names iron, steel, cobalt and nickel as the magnetic materials needed. But they are not the only ferromagnetic materials: gadolinium and many alloys, including the neodymium alloys the lesson itself lists, are also ferromagnetic. The same overstatement appears in revisionCardBullets[3]: 'iron, steel, cobalt, nickel only'.

factual_errors.text: A field line shows the direction a free north pole would move.
factual_errors.correction: The field direction is 'the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point'. A free pole would not necessarily follow the field line.

factual_errors.text: line up hydrogen atoms in the body
factual_errors.correction: MRI aligns the magnetic moments of hydrogen nuclei (protons), not whole atoms.
